The word turnoff has two distinct meanings — one literal and one figurative. Both are common in everyday English.
Meaning 1: A place where you exit a main road

A turnoff is a spot on a road where you leave the main path and take a smaller road, a side road, or an exit that branches off in a different direction.

Think of it like this: you are driving on a big highway, and there is a point where a smaller road splits away from it, leading you toward a town, a destination, or a different route. That splitting point — the place where you "turn off" the main road — is called a turnoff.

Examples:

  • "The turnoff for the beach is about five kilometers ahead — don't miss it."
  • "He almost passed the turnoff because it had no sign."
  • "Take the second turnoff after the bridge."

The key idea here is leaving a larger road to enter a smaller one. The turnoff is not the entire smaller road — it is specifically the point of departure, the place where the two roads diverge and you choose to exit.

You will hear this word most often in driving directions and road navigation.
Meaning 2: Something that kills your interest, attraction, or enthusiasm

This is the more widely used meaning in casual conversation. A turnoff is anything — a behavior, a quality, a habit, a sight, a smell, a situation — that makes you suddenly lose interest, feel repelled, or become less attracted to something or someone.

The logic of the word is simple: imagine your interest or enthusiasm as something that is "turned on" (like a switch). A turnoff switches it off. It kills the positive feeling you had.

Examples:

  • "He seemed attractive at first, but his constant bragging was a huge turnoff."
  • "The restaurant looked beautiful, but the smell near the kitchen was a real turnoff."
  • "For many voters, the candidate's aggressive tone was a turnoff."
  • "Rudeness is an instant turnoff for her — she simply walks away."

This meaning applies across many situations:

  • Romantic/personal attraction — This is where the word is most commonly used. A turnoff is something that makes a person less romantically or physically attracted to someone else. It is the opposite of a turn-on (something that increases attraction or interest).
    • "She finds overconfidence a major turnoff in a partner."
  • General interest or enthusiasm — A turnoff can also describe something that discourages you from pursuing or enjoying anything, not just a person.
    • "The high price was a turnoff — I decided not to buy it."
    • "The aggressive sales tactics were a turnoff; I left without looking at anything."
  • Social or professional settings — Certain behaviors in public or at work can be called turnoffs too.
    • "Interrupting people constantly is a turnoff in a job interview."
The core idea behind both meanings

Both meanings share the same underlying image: something that causes you to deviate from your current path or direction — either physically (you leave the main road) or emotionally/mentally (you leave behind your interest or attraction).

In meaning 1, the turnoff is neutral — it is simply a road feature.
In meaning 2, the turnoff carries a negative charge — it is something unwelcome that pushes you away.

A turnoff can be mild or severe, depending on how strongly it repels you. Notice how speakers use intensifiers to signal this:

  • "It was a bit of a turnoff." (mild — it slightly reduced my enthusiasm)
  • "It was a real turnoff." (moderate — it genuinely bothered me)
  • "It was a massive/huge/instant turnoff." (strong — it completely killed my interest)

• It is not just something you dislike in passing. A turnoff specifically diminishes attraction, enthusiasm, or willingness to engage with something or someone.
  • It is not a permanent judgment. You might have one turnoff about a person but still like them overall. The word describes a reaction to a specific thing, not a total verdict.

Picture a light switch. Your interest, enthusiasm, or attraction is the light — it is on. A turnoff is the thing that flips that switch to off. The light goes out. That reaction — the moment the switch flips — is what the word captures.
